subtype: Processions and ceremonial movement [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Parveen, and I was walking with Pankaj through the old town in Kochi when we heard drums and a brass band coming round the corner. Pankaj, just arrived from Delhi, grinned and pulled out his phone. "A wedding! Let's film the baraat!" Then the procession came into view. Men in white walked slowly behind a flower-covered bier. The band played, but the faces were still and wet-eyed. Pankaj lowered his phone, his grin fading. He looked at me, confused. I wasn't sure either; I'd grown up in Kerala but never in this community. We stepped back against a shop wall. The shopkeeper, an old man, said quietly, "An old teacher. Ninety-two. The band is for a full life." Pankaj nodded and put his phone away. He stood with his hands folded until the procession passed. I don't know exactly what he felt, but he was silent for the next ten minutes.

qa.q: How old was the teacher who had died?
qa.a: Ninety-two.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling as the procession came into view?
qa.a: His fading grin and lowered phone suggest he felt confused and embarrassed, realising it was a funeral, not a wedding.

qa.q: What did Pankaj and Parveen do that showed respect?
qa.a: They stepped back, Pankaj put his phone away and folded his hands, and they asked the shopkeeper instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did the shopkeeper explain the band?
qa.a: He said the band was for a full life, since the old teacher was ninety-two.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult reading a procession as a wedding, then learning it was a funeral, and watching respectfully and asking.

subtype: Processions and ceremonial movement [Interpreting]
passage:
Day one. On Varun's first week in Lucknow for his internship, he heard slow drumming and saw people in black walking through the old city at night, some beating their chests. He assumed it was a festival and asked a passer-by, "Which celebration is this?" The man looked at him sadly and walked on. Varun's face burned.
Day two. He asked Vidya, his colleague who had grown up in the old city. "It's Muharram," she said gently. "For many Shia families it's a time of mourning, remembering a great loss in their history. It isn't a celebration." Varun felt awful about his question.
Day four. Vidya took him to watch the procession from her aunt's balcony. Varun stayed quiet, watching the black flags and the faces. When a young man looked up, Varun bowed his head slightly. Vidya's aunt offered him sherbet. "You came to understand," she said. "That's respect."

qa.q: Where did Vidya take Varun to watch the procession?
qa.a: From her aunt's balcony.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling after the passer-by walked away?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face burning, realising his question may have hurt someone in mourning.

qa.q: What did Varun do that helped him understand?
qa.a: He asked Vidya, who knew the tradition, and then watched quietly and respectfully from the balcony.

qa.q: How did Vidya's aunt see Varun's presence at the procession?
qa.a: She saw it as respect, because he came to understand rather than to watch for fun.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a mourning procession as celebration and learning to observe respectfully and ask.

subtype: Processions and ceremonial movement [Interpreting]
passage: Jagdish, since you're going to Scotland for your master's, let your Harsha uncle tell you a story. When I was twenty-one, I went to Edinburgh on a short exchange. On my first Saturday I heard bagpipes, slow and wailing, and saw a long line of people in black gowns walking two by two up the hill. I thought someone important had died. I took off my cap, stood very still by the road and bowed my head. A girl in a gown broke line, laughed and handed me a flyer. "It's graduation! We're celebrating!" I felt so foolish. For us, that slow wailing music sounds like mourning. For them, it was pride. That evening I asked my hostel warden to explain the robes, the colours and the march. He talked for an hour, delighted that I asked. Watch first, beta. Then ask. The music doesn't always mean what it means at home.

qa.q: What did the girl hand young Harsha?
qa.a: A flyer.

qa.q: How did young Harsha feel when the girl said it was graduation?
qa.a: He felt foolish and embarrassed, having taken the slow bagpipes and black gowns as signs of mourning.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Harsha understand the march?
qa.a: That evening he asked his hostel warden to explain the robes, colours and march, instead of just guessing.

qa.q: How did the girl in the gown see Harsha's bowed head?
qa.a: She found it funny, laughing and handing him a flyer to explain it was a celebration.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading a graduation march as a funeral and learning that tradition sets the meaning, so observing and asking helps.

subtype: Public demonstrations and peaceful protest [Expressing]
passage: I'm Chinmay, and I went with Bhavna to the march for better street lighting outside our campus after two students were mugged near the bus stop. She had painted a sign: "LIGHT THE ROAD." At the gathering point, before the march began, I saw her check the route map the organisers had shared and point out the side lane near the temple. "If it gets messy, we go there," she said. We walked slowly, chanting "Safe roads, bright roads!" Bhavna's voice was clear and steady. Near the main gate, a group of men from outside the college began shouting and pushing. Bhavna's face tightened. She didn't shout back. She tapped my arm, and we moved to the side lane with three others. From there we watched the organisers talk to the police, and the march continued peacefully. Later, she posted photos of the sign, not the fight.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's sign say?
qa.a: "LIGHT THE ROAD."

qa.q: What might Bhavna have been feeling when the men began shouting and pushing?
qa.a: Her tightened face suggests she felt worried and tense, but she stayed calm and determined, choosing to move away rather than shout back.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do to stay safe while protesting?
qa.a: She checked the route and an exit lane before the march, and moved to it with others when the pushing started.

qa.q: How did Chinmay see Bhavna during the march?
qa.a: Chinmay saw her as clear and steady, chanting calmly and making sensible choices when things turned tense.

grounding: Shows through an observer a young adult expressing a concern through peaceful protest while staying aware of safety and exit routes.

subtype: Public demonstrations and peaceful protest [Expressing]
passage:
Monday. The ward's water supply in Aurangabad had failed for three weeks. Shankar and his friend Devika decided to join the residents' march to the municipal office on Thursday. That evening Shankar read the permission letter the residents' committee had got from the police and noted the route.
Thursday. Two hundred people walked with empty pots, chanting "Paani do!" Shankar held one end of the banner; Devika held the other. When the road narrowed near the bridge and the crowd bunched, Shankar remembered the side street the committee had marked. He guided a group of older women that way. Devika kept the chant going.
Saturday. The municipal commissioner met a committee of five, and a tanker came to the ward that evening. Shankar was proud, but tired. "I didn't know shouting slogans could feel so calm," he said. Devika laughed. "Because we had a plan."

qa.q: What did the marchers carry?
qa.a: Empty pots.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling after the march?
qa.a: He felt proud of what they achieved, but also tired from the effort.

qa.q: What preparations made the march safer?
qa.a: Reading the police permission letter, knowing the route and a side street to use when the crowd bunched.

qa.q: How did Devika see the calm feeling during the march?
qa.a: Devika thought it came from having a plan in advance.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing a concern through a peaceful march while staying aware of rules and exit routes.

subtype: Public demonstrations and peaceful protest [Expressing]
passage: Hafsa, you're asking if you should go to the march on Saturday. Let your Rehana Khala tell you about mine. I was twenty, a college student in Hyderabad, when a girl from our hostel was attacked on her way home. We were so angry. Thirty of us made candles and posters and walked from the college to the police station, silent, just holding the candles. Silence felt stronger than shouting. Before we left, our warden, a strict woman, made us write her number on our wrists and told us the lanes to use if anything went wrong. Halfway there, some boys on bikes started jeering. I felt my heart pound, but we did what she'd said: stayed together and didn't answer. At the police station, the inspector came out and met us. Go, beti. Just go with friends, know your way out, and remember your voice matters most when it's calm.

qa.q: What did the warden make the students write on their wrists?
qa.a: Her number.

qa.q: How did young Rehana feel when the boys on bikes started jeering?
qa.a: She was frightened, her heart pounding, but stayed calm and kept to the plan with the others.

qa.q: What choice inside the story kept the march safe and peaceful?
qa.a: The students stayed together and didn't answer the jeering, following the warden's instructions about lanes and her number.

qa.q: How did the warden treat the march?
qa.a: She supported it but planned for safety, giving them her number and exit lanes before they left.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing concern through a peaceful silent march while staying aware of safety and exits.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage:
Day one. On Baljeet's first evening in the Chennai hostel, far from Ludhiana, a girl from the next room, Rukmini, knocked with a steel box. "Murukku. My Amma's. Welcome." Baljeet was surprised, unsure if it was just politeness.
Day three. Rukmini knocked again, this time to invite her to the hostel's Pongal lunch. Baljeet hesitated, thinking she'd be in the way. Rukmini laughed. "No, no, you're coming. You're one of us now." At the lunch, three girls showed her how to eat off the banana leaf with her fingers. Baljeet felt her shoulders loosen for the first time since arriving.
Day ten. Baljeet's mother sent a box of pinnis from home. Baljeet went door to door with them, starting with Rukmini. "Thank you for the murukku. And for Pongal." Rukmini bit into one and closed her eyes. "Now we're even," she grinned. "But you're still coming to Karthigai."

qa.q: What did Rukmini first bring Baljeet?
qa.a: Murukku, her Amma's.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel at the Pongal lunch?
qa.a: She felt her shoulders loosen and felt welcome and at ease for the first time since arriving.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that returned the welcome?
qa.a: She shared her mother's pinnis door to door, starting with Rukmini, and thanked her for the murukku and Pongal.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see her gifts and invitations?
qa.a: As a real welcome, telling Baljeet she's one of them now and inviting her to the next festival.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new hostel reading shared sweets and invitations as warm welcome and returning it in her own way.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: Anjali beta, you're moving to Pune next week, so listen to your Pooja Mausi. When I was nineteen, I moved to Shillong for college, alone, into a rented room. The very first evening, the landlady's daughter came up with a plate of rice cakes and tea, and asked me a hundred questions. Where was I from, did I have brothers, did I eat pork? I thought she was nosy. I gave short answers and shut the door. The next week, the neighbours invited me to a Christmas dinner, and I almost made an excuse. Then my classmate Iba told me, "In our families, feeding you and asking about your family is how we say welcome." I felt so small. So I went, and I brought laddoos from home. They sang, they fed me, and I stayed till midnight. Take the tea, beta. The questions are the welcome.

qa.q: What did the landlady's daughter bring on the first evening?
qa.a: A plate of rice cakes and tea.

qa.q: How did young Pooja feel after Iba explained the questions?
qa.a: She felt small and ashamed of having read the kind questions as nosiness.

qa.q: What choice in the story opened the door to friendship?
qa.a: Young Pooja chose to go to the Christmas dinner and brought laddoos, instead of making an excuse.

qa.q: How did the neighbours seem to feel when young Pooja came?
qa.a: They were warm and welcoming, singing and feeding her until midnight.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new city learning to read food and questions as signs of welcome shaped by local custom.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: Lavanya arrived at Pune station at eleven at night in pouring rain, and her suitcase had gone to Mumbai by mistake. She stood soaked outside her new paying-guest building, holding only a backpack. The owner's son, Chetan, came down with an umbrella. "Come in. Amma says you'll eat with us tonight." Lavanya hesitated. She didn't want to be a burden; at home you'd refuse at least twice. "No, no, I'll manage." Chetan laughed. "In this house, if you refuse, Amma will send food to your room anyway." Upstairs, his mother handed her a dry towel, a borrowed kurta and a plate of hot poha. "You're our guest first, tenant later." Lavanya felt her eyes sting. She thanked them again and again. Chetan's mother waved it away. "Just say it once. Then eat." The next morning, Chetan went with her to the courier office to chase the suitcase.

qa.q: Where had Lavanya's suitcase gone by mistake?
qa.a: To Mumbai.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when Chetan's mother gave her the towel and poha?
qa.a: She was moved and grateful, her eyes stinging, after arriving soaked and alone.

qa.q: What helped Lavanya read the invitation as real welcome?
qa.a: Chetan's joke that his mother would send food anyway, and the warm, practical care upstairs.

qa.q: How did Chetan's mother see Lavanya's repeated thanks?
qa.a: She waved it away, suggesting in her family thanks is said once, and care doesn't need repeated gratitude.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new city under difficult circumstances reading invitations and food as welcome, with custom shaping how thanks is voiced.

subtype: Loving and admiring in adult relationships [Expressing]
passage:
"You never say you love me," Sahil said, sitting on the steps outside the library.
Ira looked up from his notes, which she'd been highlighting for him. "What?"
"You text 'ok' and 'reached'. That's it."
"Sahil, I just spent two hours making your revision notes. Yesterday I fixed your cycle. Last week I sat with your Nani at the hospital."
"I know. I noticed. But I need to hear it sometimes."
Ira was quiet. "At home, nobody says it. We just do things."
"At mine, Mummy says it ten times a day."
"So what feels caring to you? Tell me."
He thought. "A message in the day. Just one line. And sometimes, you know, the words."
"And what feels caring to you?" he asked.
"Honestly? When you show up. Like with the cycle."
She handed him the notes. "Okay. One line a day. Even if it feels strange."

qa.q: What did Ira fix for Sahil yesterday?
qa.a: His cycle.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he said Ira never says she loves him?
qa.a: He felt a little hurt and unsure, needing to hear the words even though he noticed all she did.

qa.q: What did Ira and Sahil do that helped?
qa.a: They asked each other what feels caring instead of assuming, and agreed on a small change, one line a day.

qa.q: How does Ira see love?
qa.a: For Ira, love is shown through actions like revision notes, fixing the cycle and sitting with Nani, as in her home where nobody says it.

grounding: Shows young adults expressing love through time, help and messages, and asking each other what feels caring instead of assuming.

subtype: Loving and admiring in adult relationships [Expressing]
passage: Looking back at my first year as a junior engineer, what I remember most is how much I admired Mridul sir. I'm Madhav. He wasn't loud or showy. He just stayed calm when a machine broke and asked everyone what they'd seen before fixing it. I wanted to be like that. So I started watching how he did things. I copied his habit of writing three bullet points before any meeting. I asked if I could shadow him on site visits. Once, after a hard audit, I told him, a bit shyly, "Sir, I've learned more from watching you than from my whole degree." He looked surprised, then smiled and said, "Then ask me more questions. Watching is half." After that I brought him a question every Friday. I think admiration is a kind of love, in a way: you want to grow into what you see in someone.

qa.q: What habit did Madhav copy from Mridul sir?
qa.a: Writing three bullet points before any meeting.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when telling Mridul sir about learning from him?
qa.a: Madhav felt shy and a little nervous, but full of admiration and respect for the mentor.

qa.q: What did Mridul sir suggest, and why did it help Madhav grow?
qa.a: He suggested asking more questions, because watching is only half, so Madhav brought him a question every Friday.

qa.q: How did Mridul sir react to Madhav's words?
qa.a: He looked surprised and then smiled, suggesting he was touched and pleased.

grounding: Shows a young adult expressing admiration by learning from a mentor and asking what helps, as a form of care.

subtype: Loving and admiring in adult relationships [Expressing]
passage:
Facilitator's note, community centre workshop on friendship and care, Saturday.
Today's pair exercise asked each person to describe how they show care. Mehak and Vandana, best friends for ten years, were sure they knew each other. Mehak said she shows love by planning surprises and sending long voice notes. Vandana said she shows love by remembering small things and turning up with food when someone is ill. Then I asked each to say what makes them feel cared for. Mehak said, "When someone just sits with me, no phones." Vandana said, "Long voice notes, actually. I replay them." They both laughed; each had been giving what she herself liked, not what the other needed most. Mehak admitted she'd felt a little neglected last month when Vandana dropped off soup but didn't stay. They agreed to try the other's way for a month. A good reminder for everyone: people feel cared for in different ways, and it helps to ask.
— Nandita

qa.q: How long have Mehak and Vandana been best friends?
qa.a: For ten years.

qa.q: How had Mehak felt last month when Vandana dropped off soup?
qa.a: She had felt a little neglected, because Vandana didn't stay and sit with her.

qa.q: What did the exercise help Mehak and Vandana do?
qa.a: It helped them ask what makes each feel cared for, and agree to try the other's way for a month.

qa.q: How does Vandana feel about Mehak's long voice notes?
qa.a: She treasures them, replaying them, which shows those notes make her feel cared for.

grounding: Shows young adults learning that love styles differ in close relationships and that asking what feels caring is better than assuming.

subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]
passage: Aadhya had been teaching at the girls' school in Rajgarh for four months when her grandmother died back in Kochi. The bus and train would take two days; the funeral was the next morning. She told the headmistress quietly and went to her class anyway, because the exams were near. She smiled at the students and wrote on the board. Only her colleague Irfan noticed her hand shaking with the chalk. At lunch he found her alone in the staff room. "Aadhya ma'am, you don't have to pretend here." Her face crumpled. She told him about her grandmother's garden, the jackfruit tree. Irfan listened. That evening, in her rented room, she lit a lamp beside Ammamma's photo at the same hour as the funeral, and her mother held her phone up so Aadhya could see the rites. The next day Irfan left the number of the district counselling helpline on her desk, with a note: "In case the evenings get long."

qa.q: Where had Aadhya been teaching?
qa.a: At the girls' school in Rajgarh.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling as she taught her class that day?
qa.a: She was grieving and trying to hide it with a brave face; her shaking hand showed how much she was holding in.

qa.q: What helped Aadhya begin to heal while far from home?
qa.a: Talking to Irfan, lighting a lamp at the hour of the funeral while watching the rites by phone, and having the counselling helpline number.

qa.q: How did Irfan notice Aadhya's grief?
qa.a: He saw her hand shaking with the chalk, even though she was smiling at the students.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving far from home behind a brave face, and finding support through a colleague, a ritual and counselling resources.

subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]
passage: The call came at 3 a.m. in Madrid: Siddiq's father had died in Srinagar. The funeral would be that same afternoon, and no flight could get him there in time. He sat on the kitchen floor, not crying, just staring. In the morning he told his flatmate Valentina, "I'm fine. I've got a lecture." She didn't believe him. "Siddiq, you don't have to be fine." He shook his head and went to the lecture anyway. That evening Valentina found the address of the nearest mosque and sat with him on the bus. The imam, hearing, gathered the evening worshippers to offer the funeral prayer in his father's absence. Siddiq cried for the first time as he stood in the line. Afterwards Valentina said the university had a counsellor who spoke Urdu. He wrote down her name. "Tomorrow," he said. "I'll go tomorrow." She nodded and made him tea when they got home.

qa.q: What time did the call come?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when he said "I'm fine"?
qa.a: He was in shock and grieving, putting on a brave face and staring instead of crying.

qa.q: What helped Siddiq mark his loss far from home?
qa.a: Valentina went with him to the mosque, where the imam led the funeral prayer in his father's absence, and she found him a counsellor.

qa.q: How did Valentina read Siddiq's "I'm fine"?
qa.a: She didn't believe it, seeing that he was hiding deep grief behind a brave face.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving far from family behind a brave face and finding support through ritual, a friend and counselling.

subtype: Grieving and sorrowful away from home [Regulating]
passage: In the university hostel common room in Hyderabad, Dolma had been laughing too loudly at the television all week. Her childhood friend in Gangtok had died in a landslide, and she hadn't been able to go home. She told everyone she was fine. Naveen, the student hostel representative, had seen her sitting alone on the stairs at 2 a.m. twice. On Friday evening he sat down near her, not too close. "Dolma, I heard about your friend. I'm really sorry." She stared at the screen. "I'm fine." "You don't have to be. Would it help to do something for her? Some people light a butter lamp, or write her a letter." Dolma's eyes filled. "We used to write letters in school." She talked about her friend for an hour. Before she went to bed, Naveen gave her the timings of the university counselling centre, and she booked a slot for Monday morning.

qa.q: Where did Dolma's friend die?
qa.a: In a landslide, in Gangtok.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling beneath the loud laughter?
qa.a: She was grieving deeply and trying to hide it, which showed in the late nights alone on the stairs.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that supported Dolma?
qa.a: He sat with her gently, acknowledged the loss, suggested a way to mark it, listened, and gave her the counselling centre timings.

qa.q: What would change if Naveen had believed Dolma's "I'm fine"?
qa.a: Dolma might have kept grieving alone at night, without talking about her friend or booking the counselling slot.

grounding: Shows a young adult grieving far from home behind a brave face, and a peer encouraging ritual, talk and counselling.

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage:

Pankaj: small thing but I'd rather say it now than explode later lol

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: The group project at the polytechnic in Hoshangabad was due in ten days, and Kamal had missed three meetings. Each time Kiran sent a message; each time Kamal replied, "Sorry, coming next time." By the fourth meeting, Kiran felt the anger building: jaw tight, words sharp in her head. She almost typed, "You're useless." Instead she walked twice round the college ground, bought a lime soda, and waited till her breathing slowed. Then she called him. "Kamal, I'm frustrated. We've met four times and you've come to none. I need to know if you can do the wiring section by Friday, or if we should split it differently." There was a pause. "My father's shop assistant quit. I've been at the counter every evening." Kiran's anger softened. "Can you do mornings?" "Yes." "Then let's meet at eight tomorrow." He came, and did his part.

qa.q: How many meetings had Kamal missed before Kiran called?
qa.a: Three meetings; he had come to none of the four.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling before she called Kamal?
qa.a: She was angry and frustrated, her jaw tight and harsh words in her head.

qa.q: What helped Kiran avoid turning irritation into a fight?
qa.a: Taking a break to walk and calm down, then naming the issue calmly with a clear request.

qa.q: What was Kamal dealing with that Kiran didn't know?
qa.a: His father's shop assistant had quit, so he had been working at the counter every evening.

grounding: Shows a young adult calming building anger with a break and naming a group project issue in calm words before it becomes conflict.

subtype: Angry and irritated in shared living and study [Regulating]
passage: Nkechi had been sharing a flat in London with Wanjiru for two months, and the late-night phone calls were wearing her down. Every night, past midnight, Wanjiru's laugh came through the thin wall. Nkechi lay awake, getting angrier, rehearsing a speech. One morning she caught herself slamming the kettle down. That scared her. She didn't want to be the person who slammed things. So that evening, when they were both cooking, she said, "Can I mention something small before it becomes big? The calls after midnight wake me up, and I've got early shifts. Could you take them in the kitchen after twelve, or keep them shorter?" Wanjiru winced. "Oh no, I didn't realise the wall was that thin. My family's in Nairobi, it's the only time they're free." "The kitchen, then?" "The kitchen. And I'll use earphones." That night, Nkechi slept through.

qa.q: Where is Wanjiru's family?
qa.a: In Nairobi.

qa.q: What was Nkechi feeling before she spoke up?
qa.a: She was angry and worn down from lost sleep, and scared by how she slammed the kettle.

qa.q: Why was raising it early and calmly a good choice?
qa.a: It let Nkechi explain the problem before anger took over, and they found a simple fix together.

qa.q: How did Wanjiru react to Nkechi's request?
qa.a: She winced, apologised for not realising the wall was thin, explained her family's timing, and agreed to use the kitchen and earphones.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing irritation building in shared living and naming the issue early with calm words.

subtype: Fearful and alarmed in unsafe situations [Interpreting]
passage: At the university library in Kolkata, Tanuja stayed till the 10 p.m. closing bell. On the stairs she noticed a man she'd seen by the shelves earlier, now behind her. When she slowed, he slowed. When she turned onto the dark path to the hostel, his footsteps turned too. Her stomach knotted and her skin prickled. Maybe he was just a student going the same way. But she didn't wait to find out. She turned back towards the lit entrance, where the security guard sat, and stood by his desk. She texted her friend Damini: "Someone following me from library. At security desk." Damini replied within seconds: "Stay there, coming with Mona." The guard looked up. "Everything okay, madam?" Tanuja told him. The man walked past slowly and went towards the main gate. The guard noted the time, and Damini arrived and walked her back to the hostel.

qa.q: Where did Tanuja go when she felt followed?
qa.a: Back to the lit entrance, by the security guard's desk.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling on the dark path?
qa.a: She was afraid and uneasy, her stomach knotting and skin prickling, though she knew he might just be going the same way.

qa.q: What steps did Tanuja take that were sound?

subtype: Fearful and alarmed in unsafe situations [Interpreting]
passage:
Dear Salma,
Something happened at the station yesterday and I want to tell you, because you always tell me to trust my gut.
A man came up to me near the ticket counter, very friendly, and said he had a job for me: "Data entry, great pay, start today." He kept standing too close, and when I said I'd think about it, he said, "Only today. My car is outside. Come now, don't tell your family, they'll just worry." Everything in my body went cold.
Maybe he was just a pushy recruiter. I don't know. But "now" and "don't tell your family" made my heart race. I walked straight to the railway police booth and told the constable. She took down his description and said I'd done the right thing. Then I called Ammi.
I'm fine. Just shaken. I'm telling you so you know the signs too.
Santosh

qa.a: Straight to the railway police booth.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when the man said "don't tell your family"?
qa.a: Santosh felt alarmed and scared, going cold with a racing heart, and was left shaken afterwards.

qa.q: What did Santosh do that was wise?
qa.a: Santosh treated the unease as a warning cue, left the man, reported it to the railway police and told family.

qa.q: How did the constable respond to Santosh's report?
qa.a: She took down the man's description and said Santosh had done the right thing.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing pressure and a gut sense of danger, and leaving and reporting rather than going along.

subtype: Fearful and alarmed in unsafe situations [Interpreting]
passage: Akash, you asked for the scariest night of my college life, for your podcast. I'm Zubin. It was after a birthday party at a farmhouse outside the city. Around one, a senior I barely knew, clearly drunk, jangled his keys and said, "Come, I'll drop you. Everyone's leaving." Two others were already getting in. Something in my gut said no. His eyes were glazed, he was swaying, and when I hesitated he got angry. "What, you don't trust me?" My hands went cold. I made an excuse about waiting for a friend, walked back inside to where the host's mother was sitting, and told her. She took the keys off him, called cabs for all of us and made everyone wait in the living room. I still don't know if I was right about everything. But leaving was right.

qa.q: Where was the birthday party?
qa.a: At a farmhouse outside the city.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when the drunk senior got angry?
qa.a: Zubin felt afraid, hands going cold, with a strong gut sense that getting in the car was unsafe.

qa.q: What steps did Zubin take that were sound?
qa.a: Zubin made an excuse, went back inside to a responsible adult and told her, instead of getting in the car.

qa.q: How did the host's mother respond when Zubin told her?
qa.a: She took the keys, called cabs for everyone and made them wait inside.

grounding: Shows a young adult treating a gut sense of danger as a cue and choosing to leave and ask for help.

subtype: Sympathetic and reassuring toward peers [Expressing]
passage: Rekha, you asked what to say to your friend who's struggling. Let your Yusuf mama tell you what I learnt at twenty. My friend Amir failed his final year. I did what I thought friends do: I gave advice. "Reappear next term. Make a timetable. Don't waste time crying." He stopped answering my calls. My mother said, "You talked. Did you listen?" So I went to his house, sat on the floor next to him, and said nothing for a long time. Finally he said he felt like he'd let his whole family down. I didn't argue. I just said, "That sounds so heavy." He cried, and I stayed. Weeks later, when he told me he couldn't eat or sleep at all, I said, "I think a doctor or counsellor should know." We went together the next morning. Listening first, beti. Advice later. And when it's serious, bring in someone trained.

qa.q: What did young Yusuf's mother ask him?
qa.a: "You talked. Did you listen?"

qa.q: How did Amir feel after failing his final year?
qa.a: He felt heavy and ashamed, as if he had let his whole family down.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Yusuf supported Amir?
qa.a: His mother's question made him go and sit with Amir quietly and listen, and later take him to a counsellor when things became serious.

qa.q: How did Yusuf's mother see his first way of helping?
qa.a: She saw that he had talked instead of listening, which is why she asked him that question.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to sit with and listen to a distressed friend rather than give quick fixes, and to involve professionals when serious.

subtype: Sympathetic and reassuring toward peers [Expressing]
passage: The last bus from the college back to the city left at 9:40, and it was already 9:15 when Yusuf found Mridul sitting on the steps behind the exam hall, shaking. He had just seen his results: two subjects failed. His breath came fast and short. Yusuf's first instinct was to say, "It's fine, you'll clear them next time." He stopped himself. He sat down beside Mridul. "I'm here. You don't have to talk." Mridul gasped, "I can't breathe properly." Yusuf breathed slowly with him, counting out loud. After a few minutes, Mridul's breathing eased. "My father's going to be so disappointed." Yusuf didn't argue. "That's a lot to carry." They missed the 9:40. Yusuf called his elder brother to pick them up. On the way home, Mridul said, "Thanks for not telling me it's fine." Yusuf nodded, and texted the college counsellor's email to him for the morning.

qa.q: When did the last bus leave?
What was Yusuf feeling when he first found Mridul shaking?
qa.a: He was likely worried and tempted to reassure quickly, but he held back and chose to sit with Mridul.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that helped more than advice?
qa.a: He sat with Mridul, breathed with him, listened without arguing, stayed even if it meant missing the bus, and shared the counsellor's email.

qa.q: How did Mridul experience Yusuf's support?
qa.a: He was grateful, thanking Yusuf for not telling him everything was fine.

grounding: Shows a young adult sitting with a distressed friend, listening without quick fixes, under time pressure.

subtype: Sympathetic and reassuring toward peers [Expressing]
passage: It was past eleven in the Bengaluru hostel when Pallavi noticed Kashish sitting on her bed in the dark, not scrolling, not sleeping. Kashish had been quiet for weeks. Pallavi sat next to her. "Want company?" Kashish shrugged. After a long silence she said, "Sometimes I don't want to wake up tomorrow." Pallavi's heart thudded. She didn't argue or panic. "Thank you for telling me. I'm staying right here with you." She listened as Kashish talked about exams, her parents, feeling empty. Then Pallavi said gently, "I'm worried about you, and this is bigger than me. Can we call the helpline together, right now?" Kashish hesitated, then nodded. They called from Pallavi's phone; the counsellor talked with Kashish for half an hour. Afterwards, with Kashish's agreement, Pallavi went to wake the warden. The warden came at once, sat with Kashish and arranged for the college counsellor first thing in the morning. Pallavi slept on Kashish's floor that night.

qa.q: When did Pallavi notice Kashish sitting in the dark?
qa.a: Past eleven.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Kashish said she didn't want to wake up?
qa.a: Pallavi was frightened, her heart thudding, but stayed calm and caring rather than panicking.

qa.q: What steps did Pallavi take that were right?
qa.a: She stayed, listened without judging, called the helpline with Kashish that night, woke the warden, and slept on her floor.

qa.q: How did the warden respond when Pallavi woke her?
qa.a: She came at once, sat with Kashish and arranged for the college counsellor first thing in the morning.

grounding: Shows a young adult listening to and sitting with a distressed friend, and involving professional help the same night when there is serious risk.

subtype: Puzzled and confused in video calls [Mismatch]
passage: Jyoti sat on the roof of her house in Rampur, the only place her phone got a signal, for her video interview with a Delhi company. Parveen, the HR interviewer, asked her about a project, and Jyoti's face froze on the screen, mouth half open. Parveen waited. Five seconds. Ten. Was Jyoti confused? Nervous? Or had the call dropped? In Jyoti's village, the signal came and went with the wind. Parveen could hear a faint dog barking. Instead of moving on, Parveen typed in the chat, "Jyoti, I can't see you moving. Can you hear me? No rush." A few seconds later Jyoti's voice came through, crackly. "Sorry, ma'am! I was thinking, and then the video stopped. Could you repeat the question?" Parveen repeated it slowly. subtype: Skeptical and questioning in learning [Regulating]
passage: The night before the physics final, a message raced through the class group: "LEAKED PAPER, 100% real, from a teacher's cousin." A blurry photo of a question sheet was attached. Preeti had four chapters left and was tempted. But she looked more closely. The paper had last year's date in the corner. The "teacher's cousin" had no name. The message was forwarded "many times". She wrote in the group: "This looks like last year's paper. Does anyone know the actual source?" Aparna, her roommate, rolled her eyes. "Everything's fake anyway. The exam's probably rigged too. Why bother studying?" Preeti shook her head. "Not everything's fake. This one is, I think. The syllabus changed this year, and there's a question here on a chapter we dropped." Aparna paused, then looked. "Huh. True." They closed the photo and went back to chapter nine.

qa.q: What date was in the corner of the paper?
qa.a: Last year's date.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she saw the leaked paper message?
qa.a: She was tempted, with four chapters left, but also doubtful once she noticed last year's date and the missing source.

qa.q: What made Preeti's skepticism fair rather than cynical?
qa.a: She checked specific evidence, like the date and the dropped chapter, and asked for the source instead of dismissing everything.

qa.q: How did Aparna's view change after Preeti's point?
qa.a: She paused, checked for herself, agreed it was true, and went back to studying.

grounding: Shows a young adult questioning a claim fairly and curiously under exam pressure, contrasted with stubborn cynicism.

subtype: Skeptical and questioning in learning [Regulating]
passage: In the Mumbai college seminar room, the lecturer showed a news article: "Students who study with music score higher." Yamini raised her hand. "How many students were in the study? And who ran it?" The lecturer smiled. "Good questions. Let's check." The article cited a survey of 40 students by a company that sells study playlists. Yamini frowned. "Then I'd want to see a bigger study before believing it." Sarita, next to her, laughed. "Studies are all fake anyway. Scientists just say what they're paid to." The lecturer turned to her. "All of them?" Sarita shrugged. "Most." Yamini said, "But then how would you know anything is true?" Sarita didn't answer. The lecturer said, "Doubt is useful when it asks for evidence. When it refuses all evidence, it stops being thinking." Yamini wrote that down. Sarita crossed her arms but looked thoughtful.

qa.q: How many students were in the survey cited by the article?
qa.a: 40 students.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when the lecturer asked "All of them?"
qa.a: She seemed defensive and a bit cornered, shrugging and crossing her arms, though later she looked thoughtful.

qa.q: Which approach to doubt worked better, and why?
qa.a: Yamini's, because she asked specific questions about sample and source and stayed open to better evidence.

qa.q: How did the lecturer see the difference between Yamini's and Sarita's doubts?
qa.a: The lecturer saw Yamini's as useful doubt that asks for evidence, and Sarita's as refusing all evidence, which stops being thinking.

grounding: Shows a young adult questioning sources fairly and curiously, contrasted with a peer's stubborn cynicism.

subtype: Skeptical and questioning in learning [Regulating]
passage:
"All news is lies, Keerthana," Darshan said, scrolling. "Every channel has an agenda."
"Some have agendas," Keerthana said. "All of them?"
"All."
"So the flood in Assam last week, that was made up?"
"No, that happened. I saw videos."
"From where?"
Darshan paused. "From news channels. And people's phones."
"So some news is true."
"Some, fine. But you can't trust anything."
"I'd say check more, not trust nothing. Who's reporting? Do other sources say the same? Are there numbers, names?"
Darshan put his phone down. "That's a lot of work."
"It's less work than believing nothing and still being scared."
He laughed. "Okay, what would change your mind about a story?"
"Evidence. Several sources. What would change yours?"
He thought for a long time. "I don't know. Maybe I should figure that out."

qa.q: What did Darshan say he saw of the Assam flood?
qa.a: Videos, from news channels and people's phones.

qa.q: What does Keerthana seem to feel about Darshan's view?
qa.a: She seems calm and curious rather than annoyed, gently challenging him with questions instead of arguing.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that made her skepticism fair?
qa.a: She questioned claims with specific checks like sources, names and numbers, and asked what evidence would change each of their minds.

qa.q: How did Darshan's view of the news shift during the talk?
qa.a: He moved from "all news is lies" to admitting some is true and wondering what would change his mind.

grounding: Shows a young adult practising fair, curious skepticism about news, contrasted with a friend's blanket cynicism.
